data.title: How Trump's energy dominance turned into hubris: Bousso
data.description:
By Ron Bousso

When Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, “energy dominance” was the bedrock of his economic and foreign policy plans. But an unpopular war with Iran and soaring household fuel costs have now made energy policy a major liability for the US president heading into next month’s midterm elections.

Ironically, it was the US position as the world's top oil and gas producer, perhaps more than anything else, that enabled Trump to pursue foreign policy goals that may turn out to be the costliest of his political career.

In the first two years of Trump’s second term, vast US oil and gas resources emboldened Washington abroad, strengthened its hand in trade disputes and underpinned a broader effort to restore US geopolitical dominance.

Yet the Iran war exposed the central weakness in that vision: dominating energy production does not mean controlling energy prices.

What began as a pursuit of US energy independence evolved into a doctrine of energy dominance. That is now looking like energy hubris.

UNLEASHING AMERICAN ENERGY

The foundations of Trump’s strategy were laid long before his return to office last year. The development of cost-effective techniques to tap the country's onshore shale basins transformed the US into the world’s largest producer of natural gas in 2009 and petroleum in 2018. By 2022, it was the leading exporter of liquefied natural gas, giving Washington unprecedented influence over global energy markets.

US crude production rose from around 5.5 million barrels per day in 2010 to nearly 14 million bpd today, around a fifth of global supplies, while the country also accounts for more than a quarter of global LNG exports. No single nation has ever occupied such a commanding position in the global energy system.

Trump sought to turn that advantage into a governing doctrine.

On his first day back in office, he declared a national energy emergency and ordered the government to “unleash American energy”, prioritising oil, gas, coal and nuclear power while sidelining renewables.

Within weeks, he made “energy dominance” official US policy, establishing the National Energy Dominance Council and reviving his familiar “drill, baby, drill” slogan as the purported cure for elevated inflation and economic anxiety. In an October 2025 proclamation, Trump summed up the philosophy as “maximum production, maximum prosperity, and maximum power”.

ENERGY POLICY IS FOREIGN POLICY

This doctrine extended far beyond domestic energy policy.

The administration’s national security strategy, published last December, explicitly linked US influence in the Western Hemisphere to energy dominance, drawing on the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine that sought to oppose European political intervention in the region.

In a little over a year, the administration wielded US oil and LNG exports in trade negotiations, promoted energy deals as part of efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war, and highlighted Greenland’s resource wealth in a push for greater influence over the Arctic territory.

The high-water mark for Trump’s energy doctrine arguably came early this year after Washington removed Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in a swift military operation.

The US subsequently took control of Venezuelan oil exports and revenues, forced through changes to the country’s hydrocarbons legislation that displaced Chinese companies, and secured an unprecedented agreement granting it access to a fifth of Venezuela’s oil reserves.

By February, Trump’s vision of building an economy and foreign policy around abundant fossil fuel resources appeared to be taking root. The US possessed not only more energy than any rival, but also the ability to use that abundance to shape trade, diplomacy and security.

Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran in late February put that doctrine to the test.

THE IRAN QUAGMIRE

The president initially claimed that the joint campaign with Israel against Iran would last only a few weeks. He also repeatedly indicated that vast US oil and gas resources, together with newfound access to Venezuela’s oil wealth, would shield the economy from any resulting spike in energy costs, which he also suggested would be brief.

Those assumptions have not aged well.

The war launched on February 28 led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of global energy supplies used to flow, triggering one of the largest energy disruptions in modern history. Middle Eastern producers cut output and rerouted exports where possible, while major importers across Asia reduced consumption.

This caused oil prices to nearly double in the first two months of the conflict, with global benchmark Brent crude peaking at $118 a barrel in March.

That was well below the record $145 reached in 2008, when Iran-related geopolitical tensions, surging Chinese demand and a weakening US dollar drove prices higher. It was also far less than many had feared, largely thanks to reduced Chinese oil imports, ample crude stocks and the surprising adaptability of global markets. But it still represented a severe shock.

Moreover, the risk premium from the Iran war is becoming entrenched. Even though crude flows from the Middle East have mostly recovered, Brent is trading around $110.

The conflict has also spread across the Middle East, pulling in most of Washington's Gulf allies, most notably the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, which have suffered multiple deadly attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis. This has upended the market’s confidence in the security of Middle Eastern crude, unravelled longstanding supply routes and sent shipping prices skyrocketing.

Trump wanted to put his stamp on global energy markets, but this was clearly not what he had in mind.

PAIN AT THE PUMP

In one respect, the 2026 energy shock has vindicated Trump’s strategy. The war cemented the US position as the world’s top supplier of crude, refined fuels and LNG, delivering enormous profits to domestic producers and exporters and allowing the US to expand its position in the global market.

Energy independence certainly offered US consumers some protection against the energy shock, particularly compared with Asian economies, where prices and demand destruction were much more extreme this year.

But that protection has been far from ironclad.

US gasoline prices at the pump climbed above $4.60 a gallon in May, the highest level since 2022, while diesel surged to a record $6.50 a gallon in September as global refining capacity was squeezed.

Those increases rapidly became a political problem for the White House as cost-of-living concerns moved to the forefront of the campaign ahead of the midterms on November 3.

The administration sought to contain the fuel-price spike by pulling almost every available lever, including easing biofuel blending mandates and, most controversially, reaching a diesel supply agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

This dynamic underscores the difference between commanding supply and controlling prices.

Oil, LNG and refined fuels are internationally traded commodities. US producers sell them at prices shaped by global supply and demand. They don’t typically reserve cheap energy for American households.

While Trump briefly floated the idea of a diesel export ban, officials ultimately rejected it. Even though a ban might have brought down domestic prices initially, it would likely have resulted in higher fuel prices over the medium term due to global market dynamics.

‘ENERGY SECURITY IS NATIONAL SECURITY’

The administration’s assertion last October that “energy security is national security” appears more relevant than ever. The Iran war has shown that cheap and reliable energy is essential for economic growth, whether it powers heavy industry or the data centres underpinning the artificial intelligence race.

But the conflict has also changed the meaning of energy security.

For countries dependent on imports, particularly many in Asia, the shock has revealed the risks of relying heavily on distant suppliers, vulnerable shipping routes and a concentrated global refining system. Their response is likely to be broader diversification: securing more suppliers, expanding domestic fossil fuel production where possible, accelerating renewable power and shifting more transport towards electricity.

That will not kick the US off its lofty energy perch, but it will likely weaken the allure of oil and gas for many countries over the coming years.

Trump likely felt emboldened to embark on the Iran war — something his predecessors had baulked at — precisely because US energy independence made a Middle East adventure seem less risky than it had when the US was heavily reliant on Gulf oil and gas.

But the conflict has, perhaps permanently, undermined Trump’s promise that energy dominance would guarantee low prices and economic security at home.

Hubris can be a dangerous thing.

data.title: France's luxury stores board up windows ahead of fresh protests
data.description:
Key points:
  • Rolex, De Beers among Parisian stores closed on day of protests
  • Luxury stores add security staffing, board up windows
  • Industry already grappling with slowing demand

By Alessandro Parodi

Luxury boutiques in France boarded up their normally glitzy windows and added guards ahead of fresh protests on Saturday, with some planning to stay closed after rioters looted shops across the country last weekend.

France, the most visited country in the world, draws large numbers of overseas shoppers seeking Chanel handbags and Hermes scarves, an important source of revenue for brands facing slowing demand.

But some decided staying open was too risky after last week's events, when rioters smashed and looted hundreds of shops in Paris, Marseille and Bordeaux.

A Rolex retailer and a De Beers store near the capital's famous Place Vendome will remain closed on Saturday, staff said, while managers at stores including Richemont-owned IWC said they would decide whether to close early depending on the intensity of the protests.

Groups including France's main student union UNEF and the Yellow Vest group, which emerged as a potent anti-establishment movement in 2018, plan to march through central Paris later on Saturday to protest against high living costs and cuts to public services.

NOT IN THE MOOD

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said on Friday that his ministry would deploy 70,000 police officers, backed by specialist units, to prevent the violence that occurred last week.

But staff at LVMH brands Louis Vuitton, Dior and Bulgari said they weren't taking any chances and security at their stores near Place Vendome had been increased for the day. Additional private security to supplement the police presence in the neighbourhood is also planned.

Nearby department store Printemps also increased its security staff, carried out safety repairs and added security measures to reinforce shop windows and entrances, a spokesperson for the store said.

Hermes finance chief Eric du Halgouet said this week the company had increased security measures at its French stores, adding it was too early to say how much impact recent events would have on business.

The image-conscious industry can ill afford further negative publicity. Consumer sentiment is gloomy worldwide and tourism is slowing as a result of the Iran war — contributing to disappointing quarterly reports at LVMH , Hermes and Kering this month.

Lidiya Shevchenko, a sales assistant at a Graziella Braccialini store, said she doubted many people would be looking to visit stores anyway during the protests.

"I suppose the mood is just as important when it comes to shopping," Shevchenko said.

One tourist who has already been put off is Cambodian Jerry Lay, who purchased several items from Louis Vuitton on the Champs-Élysées earlier this week.

"We do enjoy shopping in France, but after experiencing the protest (last Saturday), I'd say it's 50/50 whether I would consider coming back next time," Lay said.

data.title: ICRA retains eMudhra ratings, but flags regulatory and reputational risks after security breach
data.description:
Credit rating agency ICRA has retained its ratings for Bengaluru-based eMudhra Ltd after a security incident in its global website certificate business, but flagged potential reputational damage, regulatory uncertainty and risks to customer retention.

In an update dated October 23, ICRA retained its ratings at [ICRA]A (Stable)/[ICRA]A1 on the company's ₹35 crore unallocated credit limits.

The incident involved a flaw in the generation of security keys for eight intermediate authorities that verify website certificates. The issue led to browser makers blocking the affected authorities and eMudhra revoking the certificates. The company's board subsequently decided to exit the global certificate business and focus on its core enterprise solutions and other trust services.

The agency said the direct financial impact of eMudhra's decision to exit the global Secure Sockets Layer/Transport Layer Security (SSL/TLS) certificate business was likely to be limited, as it contributes about 1% of consolidated revenue.

However, ICRA cautioned that the impact could extend beyond the revenue from the business being discontinued. It said the incident could affect customer acquisition and retention in eMudhra's enterprise solutions business and overseas markets, which account for 64% of its revenue.

The agency also flagged uncertainty over the regulatory investigation and the possibility of past misuse of the weak keys, which could lead to third-party claims and further reputational damage.

ICRA said the company's net debt-free position and strong liquidity provide a cushion against the costs of exiting the business and any near-term disruption.

The company has stated that no data was breached and its Indian Digital Signature Certificate and eSign businesses remain unaffected. In an interview with CNBC-TV18 on October 22, Kaushik Srinivasan, Co-founder of eMudhra, called the cybersecurity lapse as a “one-off incident on a bad day”.

ICRA said it would continue to monitor the outcome of the regulatory review, eMudhra's business momentum and order inflows in the coming quarters.

data.title: Markets Espresso: Gabbar Singh Yeh Kehkar Gaya...Jo Darr Gaya, Wo Marr Gaya!
data.description:
Hello Espresso Lovers! We're back after what has been a very gruelling week. In cricket, we have something known as the "Commentator's Curse", where a Commentator praises a batsman or bowler and the batsman gets out the very next ball or the bowler bowls a very poor ball immediately after the praise. Human life is no different. Last Sunday, we were happy about the fact that this is supposed to be a truncated week. But the newsflow made a four-day week seem like eight, with no end in sight!

Possibly the most iconic character Hindi Cinema ever created was Gabbar Singh, Vald Hari Singh. He gave us so many memorable lines (from the fireball pen of Salim-Javed, of course), that they possibly fit into every instance in our life. As the Gen Zs would say, it is Gabbar Singh's world, and we just happen to live in it. We live in times where there is fear almost everywhere. The fear of a bear market, the fear of war, the fear of a recession, job losses - From "Zindagi ka Dusra naam Problem hai", we have transitioned to "Zindagi ka Dusra Naam Darr hai"!

Last week, we were optimistic, hopeful, relieved about a recovery taking place. That optimism and hope has been washed away in four days. The Nifty bled, but it was the broader markets that bled and some more. 99 out of 100 and 90 out of 100 - If these were our scores in Algebra and Geometry in our childhood, our parents would be really proud. But no. These are the number of stocks in the Nifty Midcap and Nifty Smallcap index respectively, which ended with losses on Friday. It was not just Friday, that's the story of the entire week. It is almost as if the bears dressed up as Gabbar Singh and demanded, "Yeh recovery, humko de de Bulls. Yeh Recovery Humko de de!"

The market may be battered and bruised, but there is one thing we have to admit. The market has depth. IPOs like Jio Platforms are proof of that. A ₹30,000 crore issue, in a weak market, where there is selling in almost every sector, ends up getting bids worth nearly ₹5 lakh crore (Ex-Anchor Book). That's putting money where the mouth is for you. Jio Platforms also went on to achieve many more records during the three-day bidding period, and next week will be even more important for the company, as the allotment takes place for eligible shareholders on Monday and the mega listing happens on Wednesday, October 28.

At the end of the day, there will be higher and lower oil prices, higher and lower bond yields, higher and lower interest rates, but what ultimately moves the market is EARNINGS. Just as KARMA is a five-letter word, EARNINGS is exactly the same word, but in seven letters. Gabbar Singh's entry sequence in Sholay shows him putting a gun to the head of his three men, and the gun doesn't fire on either of them. Put International Gemmological Institute, Tata Tele and L&T Tech instead of the three men. Good earnings, Teeno bach gaye! Reported weekly gains at a time when almost everything on the screen was red. Now replace them with Swiggy, Himadri Specialty Chemicals and KEI Industries. The street doesn't like the numbers, the gun fires on all three of them, and the result? All of them down between 20% and 25% for the week. Sazaa mili, baraabar mili.

Then comes the next fear. AI. But right now, it's not AI that is causing the fear, the theme itself is worried, scared, tense. The trade has begun to unwind. Why? Too many things to be about any one in particular. Some disappointing results, the excessive debt taken up by some companies and the yields on that debt reaching levels of distress, companies announcing more spending plans when even the current ones have not reached fruition yet, and if all of that was not enough, there is cybersecurity. Who bore the brunt of this? The retail guys. They always do. JPMorgan says retail loaded up on these semiconductor and memory chip makers last week, and they got smashed in this one. But what will retail do? They'll buy more at the earliest opportunity. They always do. Their hope and optimism sometimes put even those words to shame.

Since we were on Cybersecurity, the casualty of the week has been eMudhra. Private keys associated with its certificates were compromised. It's too technical a subject to explain in non-technical language. So we left this task to our friend Ashmit Kumar, who does it beautifully in this video. The management, though, called it a "one-off incident on a bad day." The market definitely did not think of it that way. Two straight days of 20% lower circuits and an exit from the business that the issue was associated with - the reactions to a "one-off incident on a bad day" are never so extreme. Hear out the management also speak to us on this issue and the defence they put up in this video.

Just as we have FOMO and JOMO, there should be a FODT too. The Fear Of Donald Trump. We just don't know when he wakes up and writes something on Truth Social that sends everybody around helter-skelter, announces something that nobody has a clue about, or says something outlandish in a rally that leaves people scratching their heads. Tariffs, a war that will now enter month No. 9, an election to face, and the lowest approval rating on record, the man has turned the world on its head in 2026 but remains hopeful of a Nobel Peace Prize. Think about it, jab 50-50 kos door koi ultra-bullish ya bearish ho jaata hai, to log kehte hai, bete Truth Social dekh le, Trump kuch likh dega!

We get into the business end of the earnings season next week. Multiple Nifty results, broader market names, the Fed rate decision, monthly expiries, and so much more. And then there is the market volatility and geopolitical tensions to grapple with anyway. We'll be on top of things as always. You don't need to fear about that part for sure! Subscribe to our newsletter, follow us on our social media handles, and you'll get the latest brew, the fastest and the most accurate!

Investing is difficult. Especially for smaller investors. The constant fear, especially in scenarios like these - whether the market will recover? Should I put money in now? Should I go all in or do it in a staggered way? What if the market falls more after I invest? What if the stocks I invest in fall more? But such is the market, right? And Such is life too. And who better than Gabbar Singh, Vald Hari Singh to tell us the biggest principle to overcome any fear we have, whether it be in life or for the markets - Jo Darr Gaya, Samjho Marr Gaya!
